hero.headline: Martin County could lose $67 million under proposed homestead exemption expansion
hero.teaser: A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could lower tax bills for homeowners, but critics warn renters may pay more if local governments raise rates to offset lost revenue.
hero.body:
A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could benefit homeowners while potentially raising costs for renters, according to recent analysis. The Florida Policy Institute estimates Martin County could lose more than $67 million in tax revenue if voters approve the amendment in November. Statewide, local governments could lose nearly $4.8 billion under the proposal.

The expansion raises concerns for vulnerable renters already struggling with housing costs. At Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, Executive Director Mike Readling reports that 95 percent of people seeking assistance with rent and bills are renters. "The housing situation is so dire," Readling said. "It's gotten progressively worse. We have families coming in every day." He believes the proposed tax cut would not help the organization's clients. "The demographic that we're working with and Habitat for Humanity tries to help, it's not going to help them at all," Readling said. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis found there are just 24 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income renters, highlighting the acute shortage of affordable housing.

When local governments face revenue shortfalls, they typically have limited options. Attorney John Tolley explained that municipalities could cut services, reduce reserves, or increase millage rates. If rates rise, homesteaded homeowners would still benefit from the tax exemption, but landlords without that exemption could face higher tax bills. Realtor Michael Caputo acknowledged the potential impact: "There could be an effect where we see some people getting priced out of these rentals, which are already pretty high." However, Caputo suggested that landlords facing increased costs might not immediately raise rents, and the market could stabilize through supply and demand forces. "The landlords are just going to have a flow through effect," Caputo said. "If it doesn't happen for them, then they'll have to readjust their pricing."

The amendment would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10 percent to 5 percent. Some observers see potential benefits in this provision. Tolley noted that lower property taxes could potentially lead to reduced rents. "The fact that you could have less taxes, you actually might see a trend where rents go down even further than they were before," Tolley said. Caputo added that he believes there is a high probability local municipalities may not raise millage rates at all. Despite differing perspectives, the core concern remains whether renters would ultimately bear the cost of lost tax revenue through higher housing expenses.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie distributes $24 million Waste Pro settlement via tax roll credit
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city leaders voted 4-1 to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the tax roll rather than mailing checks to residents. The tax roll distribution allows the city to send funds directly to properties using an established system. Council members also voted not to reimburse the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund.

The settlement resolves years of service failures. Resident Kelly Lee recalled neighbors experiencing overflowing garbage during the pandemic when Waste Pro failed to pick up trash. In 2021, both the company and city filed lawsuits against each other. Waste Pro blamed labor shortages while the city argued the company breached its contract for standard of service. Mayor Shannon Martin said in April after the settlement announcement that she wanted to see cash in residents' pockets. Scott Samples with the city said staff worked to collect data and create scenarios to give recommendations to council. Some residents questioned how to distribute funds fairly, noting that people who lived in the city during the trash problems have since moved away while new residents now occupy those homes.

cards.headline: Man dies in Martin County vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court
cards.teaser: A man died Saturday night when his truck caught fire off the side of the road near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court in Martin County.
cards.body:
A fatal vehicle fire that initially appeared to be the result of a crash is now being investigated as a possible accidental ignition, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. On Saturday, just after 9 p.m., deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court. When first responders arrived, they found the driver deceased inside the vehicle, burned beyond recognition.

The incident was initially treated as a traffic crash-related fire. However, after further investigation at the scene, detectives ruled out a collision as the cause, prompting the involvement of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives believe they have tentatively identified the victim and have been in contact with family members. However, due to the condition of the remains, a positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed. Those results are expected to take several weeks.

cards.headline: Attorney General Uthmeier sues TikTok over alleged violations of Florida child protection law
cards.teaser: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against TikTok on Monday, accusing the social media company of violating a 2024 state law designed to pr.
cards.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against TikTok on Monday, accusing the social media company of violating House Bill 3, a 2024 state law designed to protect minors online, as well as Florida's consumer protection statutes. The law, which took effect in January, prohibits children under 14 from having social media accounts and requires parental consent for 15- and 16-year-olds to create them. According to the complaint, TikTok is failing to comply with these requirements.

Uthmeier stated that "TikTok's success hinges on its ability to addict children and teenagers to the platform" and that the company "knowingly deceives parents and allows children to be exposed to harmful and inappropriate content in direct violation of Florida law." The lawsuit alleges TikTok misrepresents the content available on its platform, downplaying the prevalence of sexual content, drug use, profanity, self-harm and eating disorders despite marketing the app as appropriate for users 13 and older. The state also contends that TikTok engages in deceptive and unfair trade practices by misleading parents about platform safety and content moderation, while being aware of the risks posed to young users.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie council votes to distribute $24 million Waste Pro settlement via tax roll
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city leaders voted 4-1 Monday to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the tax roll rather than sending checks to residents. The tax roll option allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties using an established system. Council members also voted against reimbursing the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund. The settlement resolved lawsuits filed by both the city and Waste Pro in 2021, with Waste Pro blaming labor shortages and the city arguing the company breached its contract for standard of service.

Resident Kelly Lee, who attended Monday's meeting, recalled trash troubles during the pandemic when Waste Pro failed to pick up overflowing garbage. She raised concerns about fair distribution, noting that some residents who dealt with the trash problems have since moved while new residents now live in their homes. Lee questioned where the fair share goes for people who were present during the issues but have since relocated. Scott Samples with the city said staff have been working to collect data and create scenarios to give recommendations to city council. Mayor Shannon Martin stated in April after the settlement announcement that she was committed to making sure residents get paid back for what they endured during that time.

cards.headline: 14-year-old boy killed crossing North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach
cards.teaser: Christopher Cetoute of Boynton Beach was struck by a BMW M4 traveling at a high rate of speed as he crossed the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue on Friday night.
cards.body:
A 14-year-old Boynton Beach boy was killed Friday night after being struck by a vehicle while crossing North Congress Avenue. According to the Boynton Beach Police Department, the crash happened just before 9 p.m. on June 12 in the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue. Investigators determined that Christopher Cetoute of Boynton Beach was crossing the roadway in an eastbound direction when he was hit by a BMW M4 traveling southbound. Police said the vehicle appeared to be traveling at a high rate of speed at the time of the crash. Emergency crews from the Boynton Beach Fire Rescue responded to the scene and pronounced Cetoute dead on site.

Officials said all individuals involved remained at the scene following the crash. Authorities have not released additional details about potential charges or contributing factors. The investigation remains ongoing as detectives work to reconstruct the circumstances leading up to the collision. The Boynton Beach Police Department is asking anyone with information about the crash to come forward as the case develops. North Congress Avenue was temporarily impacted as investigators processed the scene late Friday night.

cards.headline: Tampa Mayor warns property tax amendment could cut $60 million from city budget by 2029
cards.teaser: Mayor Jane Castor is warning voters that a proposed constitutional amendment raising the homestead property tax exemption could force painful budget choices, including impacts to first responders.
cards.body:
Tampa Mayor Jane Castor is urging voters to carefully consider a proposed constitutional amendment that would increase the homestead property tax exemption, saying it could force the city to make difficult budget decisions affecting public safety services. The amendment, which state lawmakers approved for the November ballot, would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. The measure requires approval from 60% of voters to become law.

Castor emphasized that property taxes currently generate $380 million for Tampa's 2026 budget, yet this revenue barely covers the city's police and fire departments as they operate today. She projected that the amendment would reduce city property tax revenue by at least $35 million in 2028 and at least $60 million by 2029. The mayor connected the tax issue directly to public safety, noting that Tampa has hired more than 100 firefighters and 60 police officers since 2019 while crime has dropped by more than 20% during that period. "Public safety isn't optional," Castor said, suggesting these staffing increases have contributed to improved safety outcomes.

Castor raised concerns about how the city might respond to significant revenue losses, asking whether it would need to cut recreation programs or charge businesses and tax-exempt property owners public safety fees to maintain services. "Your City Council members and I already make hard budget choices every year, but this proposal could turn those into brutal choices," she said. "Do we slash recreation programs? Do we need to start charging businesses and tax-exempt property owners public safety fees to avoid cutting services? How much will the burden of funding basic government services shift toward renters and businesses?"

Tampa joins other Florida cities expressing concern about the state's property tax proposal. Supporters of the amendment argue it would provide relief to homeowners struggling with rising housing costs, insurance premiums, and tax bills. However, local government officials have warned that reducing property tax collections could either shift the financial burden to other revenue sources or require cuts to essential services. Castor called on voters to thoroughly research the proposal before voting, stating that the amendment "stands to have a tangible impact on the quality of life that has made Tampa one of America's most exciting and appealing cities."

cards.headline: Belle Glade residents raise housing and affordability concerns at library meeting
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Belle Glade residents shared stories about housing, affordability, and local resources at a Let's Hear It community meetup at the Belle Glade Library.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library during a Let's Hear It community meetup to discuss housing, affordability, local resources and upcoming events. Much of the conversation centered on affordability and housing concerns. Local activist Delories Butts asked why the community cannot help homeless people, while resident Veronica Bain shared her appreciation for where she lives.

Residents also learned about available community resources. Lavita Holmes, executive director of Glades Lives Matter, described an ambassadorship program that selects three students from every school and mentors them throughout the year. The program holds students civically responsible for attending school board meetings and commission meetings while learning about their communities. Codi Snead announced the first Juneteenth pageant in the county's history, which currently has eight contestants in grades kindergarten through fifth.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens woman receives toll bills tied to stolen temporary tag
cards.teaser: Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens repeatedly received toll bills from roads she never traveled after someone used a stolen temporary tag registered to her husband.
cards.body:
Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens received a toll bill in March for multiple tolls along Florida's Gulf Coast. The license plate number matched a temporary tag registered to her husband, but the bill referenced a black Mercedes while the Keswicks drive a white Nissan that has had a permanent tag for months. Keswick-Paine filed a report with Palm Beach Gardens Police. She expressed concern about potential liability, noting that if the person using the stolen tag committed traffic violations or hit-and-run incidents, her husband could be implicated.

Following police advice, Keswick-Paine did not pay the bill and filed a dispute with SunPass. A second invoice arrived anyway, and SunPass eventually closed the dispute without providing confirmation of resolution. After Keswick-Paine reached out to reporters in April, she received a third toll bill. Personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti said temporary tag fraud is happening frequently, while Palm Beach Gardens Police said in an email they consider the case an isolated incident. Security consultant and retired police officer Gene Petrino recommended keeping thorough records of police reports and toll disputes, and destroying temporary tags by cutting them into pieces before surrendering them. A new Florida law that took effect last year increased penalties for fraudulent use of temporary tags and made them easier for the state to track.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library launches summer reading challenge through July 31
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge with free activities and prizes.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to "Unearth a Story" this summer as part of its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31. Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen said the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs will also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

Little learners up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each branch is hosting special events from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character, at various appearances throughout the challenge.

cards.headline: Big Dog Ranch Rescue to close Wisconsin beagle facility, relocate 475 dogs to Florida
cards.teaser: Big Dog Ranch Rescue reached an agreement to permanently close Ridglan Farms in Wisconsin and transfer 475 beagles to its Florida and Alabama campuses.
cards.body:
Big Dog Ranch Rescue has reached an agreement to permanently close Ridglan Farms, a Wisconsin-based dog breeding and research facility, and transfer the remaining 475 beagles housed there. A total of 325 beagles will be transferred from Ridglan Farms to Big Dog Ranch Rescue today and tomorrow. The dogs will be transported to the organization's Florida and Alabama campuses, where they will receive medical care, including spay and neuter procedures, before being placed for adoption. Some of the beagles will also be transferred to partner rescue organizations across the country. The remaining 150 dogs are expected to be released to Big Dog Ranch Rescue by the beginning of August.

Once that transfer is complete, Ridglan Farms will permanently cease its dog breeding, sales, research and testing operations. Lauree Simmons, founder and CEO of Big Dog Ranch Rescue, asked that the public refrain from further protests directed at Ridglan Farms, its owners, or its employees. She thanked Ridglan Farms for working with the rescue organization to coordinate the transfers and for committing to permanently close its operations. The agreement follows a large-scale rescue effort carried out on April 29 that resulted in the relocation of 2,110 beagles from the facility.

hero.headline: Palm Beach Gardens woman receives toll bills from stolen temporary tag
hero.teaser: Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens has received multiple toll bills for a black Mercedes using a temporary tag registered to her husband, though they drive a white Nissan.
hero.body:
A Palm Beach Gardens resident discovered she was receiving toll bills for roads she never traveled after her husband's temporary license tag was stolen and used fraudulently. Vera Keswick-Paine first noticed the problem in March when a toll bill arrived for multiple charges along Florida's Gulf Coast. The bill displayed a license plate number matching a temporary tag registered to her husband, but it referenced a black Mercedes. The family drives a white Nissan that has carried a permanent tag for months.

Keswick-Paine reported the issue to Palm Beach Gardens Police and filed a dispute with SunPass, the state's toll collection system. However, the situation escalated beyond a simple billing error. "The guy runs a red light, the tag is in my husband's name. The guy hits and runs, tag is under my husband's name," she explained, highlighting the potential legal consequences of having someone else's crimes linked to her family's identity. Despite her efforts, a second invoice arrived, and SunPass closed the dispute without providing clear confirmation that the matter was resolved. A third toll bill came after she reached out to authorities in April.

The problem is more widespread than many realize, according to personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti. "It's happening a lot," he said. Temporary tags are attractive to criminals because they are difficult to track and allow people to drive without insurance or conduct other illegal activities without detection. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement does not maintain readily available statewide data on stolen temporary tags, which makes investigating these crimes challenging. Security consultant and retired police officer Gene Petrino described the difficulty: "It's one of those things where it's just a nightmare to follow the breadcrumbs of the crime."

Petrino recommended that people protect themselves by maintaining detailed records of police reports and toll disputes. He also advised drivers to destroy their temporary tags when transitioning to permanent plates by cutting them into pieces or removing personal information before surrendering them. Palm Beach Gardens Police characterized Keswick-Paine's case as isolated, though experts disagree about how common the problem actually is. Florida enacted a new law last year that increased penalties for fraudulent use of temporary tags and improved the state's ability to track them. Keswick-Paine's attempts to contact the Florida Department of Transportation went unanswered despite multiple follow-up inquiries over nearly a month.

cards.headline: Fire kills 4 dogs, exposes animal neglect at West Palm Beach property on 16th Street
cards.teaser: A fire inside a wooden shed at a West Palm Beach commercial property killed 4 dogs and exposed squalid living conditions for multiple animals on Monday morning.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach Fire and Police Departments responded to a fire on Monday morning at a property along the 400 block of 16th Street around 7:05 a.m. The blaze occurred inside a wooden shed on the commercial property where several dogs were locked inside. Four dogs died in the fire and another was injured.

Further investigation revealed another uninjured dog on the property, as well as 6 cats housed inside a shipping container. All animals were found living in squalor. Animal Care and Control took custody of the surviving animals, which are expected to recover from their injuries. West Palm Beach Police confirmed the property was cited on June 11, 2026, by the City of West Palm Beach Code Compliance Division for multiple property maintenance violations. The investigation remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Vanilla Ice surprises Palm Beach County deputy at awards ceremony
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office deputy Tina Izzarone got an unexpected surprise at an awards ceremony this month when rapper Vanilla Ice appeared to honor her 30 years of service.
cards.body:
Deputy Tina Izzarone was honored at the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office awards ceremony this month, celebrating 30 years of service. She received an unexpected surprise when rapper Rob Van Winkle, known as Vanilla Ice, appeared at the event. "That was amazing," Izzarone said of the moment.

The surprise was arranged by a young man named Raffie, whose connection to both the deputy and the rapper made the moment possible. The story began when Izzarone pulled over Raffie's mother during a traffic stop and noticed Raffie. "I noticed immediately of his specialness, and I made him feel really at ease knowing that his mother was not in trouble," Izzarone said. Raffie remembered the deputy's kindness and approached her again when they saw each other a few months later. Raffie has a longstanding friendship with Van Winkle, who said "Raffie and I go way back when he was a little kid and just a great honor to come out and do this." Van Winkle described his bond with Raffie, noting that when Raffie visits his house, he sits in Van Winkle's big monster truck. Adding to the moment, Van Winkle and Izzarone share the same birthday, October 31. Raffie's mother received a ticket during the original traffic stop.

hero.headline: Indian River County could lose $50 million from property tax amendment
hero.teaser: Indian River County leaders warned Friday that a property tax amendment on the November ballot could cost the county $50 million in funding by 2028.
hero.body:
Laura Moss, vice chair of the Indian River County Commission, invited neighbors and community leaders to the Heritage Center in Vero Beach on Friday morning to discuss the property tax amendment on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Moss said the state is dictating to local governments how they fund services, though each county is different and funds what the community wants.

According to the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, the county has a budget of around $597 million and predicts it could lose around $50 million in funding in 2028. Lance Lunceford, president of the association, said there is no way to fill a hole that size without eating into the county's ability to provide law enforcement and first responder services. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose around $15 to $20 million of their $70 million budget, with about 79.1 percent of funding coming from ad valorem taxes. Brewer said three projected stations may or may not happen if there is a shortfall. Lunceford said the amendment could mean raising taxes on existing tax bases like non-homesteaded and commercial properties to make up for lost revenue.

cards.headline: Belle Glade residents discuss housing concerns, community resources at library event
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Belle Glade residents came to the Belle Glade Library Monday to share stories during a Let's Hear It community meetup, focusing on housing, affordability, and local resources.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library during a Let's Hear It community meetup to discuss housing affordability, local resources, and upcoming events. Much of the conversation centered on affordability and housing challenges. Local activist Delories Butts asked why the community can't help homeless people in the area. Other residents shared their appreciation for living in Belle Glade and highlighted available resources within the community.

Lavita Holmes, executive director of Glades Lives Matter, described the organization's ambassadorship program, which selects three students from every school for year-long mentoring focused on civic responsibility, including attendance at school board and commission meetings. Holmes characterized the program as a voice for people in the Glades community. The meetup also featured discussion of upcoming events, including a historic celebration. Codi Snead announced the first Juneteenth pageant in the county's history, currently featuring eight contestants in grades kindergarten through fifth. The Let's Hear It events are designed to uncover the real stories that make communities function.

cards.headline: Daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim files wrongful death suit in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian has filed a wrongful death lawsuit after her mother Faniola Joseph and two others were killed when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck on August 12, 2025.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were traveling for work in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. All three people in the minivan were killed. Joseph, who had been living in Indiana, had come south to purchase goods to resell in her shop. Joseph's only child, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices.

Angeline is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations. Transportation expert James Lewis has described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." Bello says the case is strengthened by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims. In addition to the civil case, Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down.

cards.headline: Sara Baxter returns to Palm Beach County Commission race for District 6 seat
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the race for the District 6 Commission seat after reversing her decision to run for Congress, meeting the noon qualifying deadline.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the District 6 Commission race after reversing her decision to run for Congress, meeting the noon qualifying deadline with President Donald Trump's endorsement. Trump asked her to remain in Palm Beach County. Republican candidate Elizabeth Accomando and Democratic candidate Rudolph Tinker said the issues facing District 6 should outweigh the endorsement from the White House. "It doesn't make sense to me," Accomando said. Tinker said Baxter "lost a lot of ground and a lot of credibility as a Republican candidate." Both candidates said the focus should remain on the community's true needs.

Democratic candidates Katherine Waldron and Mario Guzman also criticized Baxter's decision. Waldron said she entered the race because District 6 needs focused leadership on traffic, neighborhood protection, quality education, and responsible growth. "Running for office is a serious commitment, not a decision that should change from one week to the next based on political circumstances or direction from Washington," Waldron said. Guzman said residents deserve "a candidate who is committed to the needs of our public" and will bring stability. The main issues facing District 6 are development, traffic, and AI data centers. The primary election is August 18, with the general election in November.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach fire kills 4 dogs, exposes animal neglect on 16th Street
cards.teaser: A fire at a West Palm Beach property Monday morning killed four dogs and exposed squalid living conditions for multiple animals on the site along the 400 block of 16th Street.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach Fire and Police Departments responded to a fire along the 400 block of 16th Street around 7:05 a.m. Monday morning. The blaze occurred inside a wooden shed on the commercial property, where several dogs were locked inside at the time. The fire killed 4 dogs and injured another.

Investigation revealed additional animals on the property living in squalid conditions: another dog that was not injured and 6 cats housed inside a shipping container. Animal Care and Control took custody of all surviving animals, which are expected to recover from their injuries. West Palm Beach Police confirm the property was cited on June 11, 2026, by the City of West Palm Beach Code Compliance Division for multiple property maintenance violations.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County deputy surprised by Vanilla Ice at awards ceremony honoring 30 years of service
hero.teaser: Deputy Tina Izzarone received an unexpected visit from rapper Vanilla Ice at a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office awards ceremony. The surprise was arranged by a young man named Raffie, who remembered the deputy's kindness during a traffic stop.
hero.body:
A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office deputy was stunned when rapper Vanilla Ice appeared at an awards ceremony recognizing her three decades of service. Deputy Tina Izzarone was being honored alongside other employees at the sheriff's office event this month when Rob Van Winkle, known professionally as Vanilla Ice, walked out to greet her. The surprise appearance left Izzarone amazed and became the highlight of the celebration.

The unexpected moment came together through a young man named Raffie, who had meaningful connections to both the deputy and the rapper. The connection began years earlier when Izzarone conducted a traffic stop involving Raffie's mother. During that encounter, Izzarone noticed something special about the young man and worked to put him at ease during the interaction. "I noticed immediately of his specialness, and I made him feel really at ease knowing that his mother was not in trouble," Izzarone said. Raffie did not forget that kindness. When the two crossed paths again a few months later, he remembered and approached the deputy to reconnect.

Raffie has also maintained a long friendship with Van Winkle that stretches back to his childhood. "Raffie and I go way back when he was a little kid and just a great honor to come out and do this," Van Winkle said. When Raffie and his mother decided to attend the awards ceremony, Raffie reached out to the rapper with an invitation. Van Winkle shared details about their bond, explaining that Raffie enjoys spending time in his monster truck whenever he visits. "I have a big monster truck and every time he comes over and every time he comes to my house he says I have to sit in it. Turns the air conditioner on and it's cool," Van Winkle said. The moment became even more meaningful when Van Winkle and Izzarone learned they share the same birthday on October 31.

The entire situation grew out of a single act of compassion shown during a routine traffic stop. Izzarone's decision to treat a young person with kindness years ago created a ripple effect that eventually led to an unforgettable surprise at her milestone career recognition. As for Raffie's mother, she did receive a ticket during that original traffic stop. But the interaction ultimately led to a story about kindness, friendship, and an unexpected celebrity appearance that brought joy to everyone involved.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office investigates fatal vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard as possible accidental ignition
cards.teaser: A driver died in a fully engulfed vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court on Saturday night. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle.
cards.body:
A fatal vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court is now being investigated as a possible accidental ignition by the Martin County Sheriff's Office. On Saturday just after 9 p.m., deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road. First responders found the driver deceased inside the vehicle, burned beyond recognition.

The incident was initially treated as a traffic crash-related fire. However, after further investigation at the scene, detectives ruled out a collision as the cause, prompting involvement of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives have tentatively identified the victim and been in contact with family members. Due to the condition of the remains, positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed, with results expected to take several weeks.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach implements youth supervision policy requiring adult chaperones
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach now requires all guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. The policy is part of the park's effort to maintain a safe environment at South Florida's largest water park.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has implemented an interim youth supervision policy requiring all guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. According to the park, the policy is part of its ongoing effort to maintain a safe and enjoyable environment for guests at South Florida's largest water park. Under the new rules, minors ages 17 and under must be accompanied by an adult chaperone, defined as a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult who is at least 21 years old and traveled to the park with the minor's group.

All adult chaperones must present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry. Chaperones must also be present when their group enters the park and remain on-site for the duration of the visit. Rapids Water Park limits each adult chaperone to supervising no more than 5 guests who are 17 years old or younger per day. Park officials said the measure aligns with the park's commitment to providing a family-friendly destination where guests can safely enjoy its attractions. The youth supervision policy is currently listed as an interim measure and is now in effect. Guests can visit Rapids Water Park's website for additional details before planning their visit.

cards.headline: 105-acre brush fire near Palm City neighborhood contained after helicopter water drops
cards.teaser: A 105-acre brush fire in Martin County is now contained after multiple agencies worked together to battle the blaze near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City.
cards.body:
A 105-acre brush fire in Martin County near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City is now contained after multiple agencies responded to the wildfire near Newfield Boulevard and Southwest Citrus Boulevard. Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Division of Forestry, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office battled the blaze as residents nearby experienced smoky conditions and increased emergency vehicle activity. The smoke and flames were visible from homes in the Newfield neighborhood, drawing crowds of onlookers.

Josh Barry, a Newfield resident who recently moved into the neighborhood a few weeks ago, said his wife alerted him to the fire from upstairs. "There was residents all over. People were lined up from all over the place watching," Barry said. Tom Hornbostel, district chief for Martin County Fire Rescue, explained how the Division of Forestry and Martin County Sheriff's Office helicopter operations helped contain the fire by picking up water from nearby lakes and performing water drops to stop the fire's progression. Although some neighbors reported seeing ash fall, fire crews said there was no threat to homes or other structures. Division of Forestry units remained on scene overnight and into Monday morning to monitor for spot-overs.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library System launches summer reading challenge through July 31
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge. The program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes through July 31.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to "Unearth a Story" this summer as part of its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running through July 31. Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen told WPTV the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

Age-specific prizes are available based on participation. Little learners up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each library branch is hosting special events ranging from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character visiting for the challenge, at various appearances. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Library launches summer reading challenge through July 31
hero.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to Unearth a Story this summer as part of its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31.
hero.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is running its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, themed "Unearth a Story," through July 31. Anyone can participate by registering at any library branch, completing an activity log and returning it to claim a prize while supplies last. Those who submit their logs also enter an automatic drawing for one of several grand prizes.

The program offers age-appropriate rewards for different groups. Children up to age 4 receive a rubber duck, while kids ages 5 to 11 can choose between a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teenagers ages 12 to 17 and adults have the option of selecting a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. All prizes are distributed on a while supplies last basis.

Beyond the core reading challenge, each library branch is hosting special events throughout the summer. These include children's story times and craft sessions alongside adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will also have opportunities to meet Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character created for the challenge, at various branch locations and special appearances.

Summer reading initiatives like this one serve an important educational purpose. According to the American Library Association, these programs help prevent the "summer slide," which refers to the decline in student learning that can occur during extended school breaks. Activity logs can be picked up and submitted at any library location. The challenge welcomes all county residents and library cardholders to participate.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast uses thrift stores for cat adoptions during Palm City shelter renovation
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily shifting many of its cats to its two thrift stores in Stuart. With shelter cages unavailable during the renovation in Palm City, spokesperson Sarah Fisher said the stores have become essential. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," she explained Thursday.

The thrift stores now offer shoppers both unique items for sale and adoptable cats. Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said donations of gently used goods are welcome and help support the animals. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted. The organization is also currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The Humane Society's thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce offers rare look at Florida's coastal ecosystems
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through rare close-up encounters with marine life in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman says the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex ecosystem models dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, distinguishing it from most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman told WPTV, noting that more species are housed here than in many larger exhibits. The Atlantic coral reef exhibit is the highlight, a sprawling tank recreating one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, including a four-inch barracuda, each demonstrating intricate relationships between organisms.

The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran. "You'll likely touch animals you've never seen before," Corcoran said. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. Operating in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, the exhibit aims to raise public awareness about ocean threats while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms. The facility is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round. More information is available at sms.si.edu.

hero.headline: Tampa Mayor warns property tax amendment could cut $60 million from city budget by 2029
hero.teaser: Mayor Jane Castor is warning voters that a proposed constitutional amendment raising the homestead property tax exemption could force painful budget choices, including impacts to first responders.
hero.body:
Tampa Mayor Jane Castor is urging voters to carefully consider a proposed constitutional amendment that would increase the homestead property tax exemption, saying it could force the city to make difficult budget decisions affecting public safety services. The amendment, which state lawmakers approved for the November ballot, would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. The measure requires approval from 60% of voters to become law.

Castor emphasized that property taxes currently generate $380 million for Tampa's 2026 budget, yet this revenue barely covers the city's police and fire departments as they operate today. She projected that the amendment would reduce city property tax revenue by at least $35 million in 2028 and at least $60 million by 2029. The mayor connected the tax issue directly to public safety, noting that Tampa has hired more than 100 firefighters and 60 police officers since 2019 while crime has dropped by more than 20% during that period. "Public safety isn't optional," Castor said, suggesting these staffing increases have contributed to improved safety outcomes.

Castor raised concerns about how the city might respond to significant revenue losses, asking whether it would need to cut recreation programs or charge businesses and tax-exempt property owners public safety fees to maintain services. "Your City Council members and I already make hard budget choices every year, but this proposal could turn those into brutal choices," she said. "Do we slash recreation programs? Do we need to start charging businesses and tax-exempt property owners public safety fees to avoid cutting services? How much will the burden of funding basic government services shift toward renters and businesses?"

Tampa joins other Florida cities expressing concern about the state's property tax proposal. Supporters of the amendment argue it would provide relief to homeowners struggling with rising housing costs, insurance premiums, and tax bills. However, local government officials have warned that reducing property tax collections could either shift the financial burden to other revenue sources or require cuts to essential services. Castor called on voters to thoroughly research the proposal before voting, stating that the amendment "stands to have a tangible impact on the quality of life that has made Tampa one of America's most exciting and appealing cities."

cards.headline: Attorney General Uthmeier sues TikTok over alleged violations of Florida child protection law
cards.teaser: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against TikTok on Monday, accusing the social media company of violating a 2024 state law designed to pr.
cards.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against TikTok on Monday, accusing the social media company of violating House Bill 3, a 2024 state law designed to protect minors online, as well as Florida's consumer protection statutes. The law, which took effect in January, prohibits children under 14 from having social media accounts and requires parental consent for 15- and 16-year-olds to create them. According to the complaint, TikTok is failing to comply with these requirements.

Uthmeier stated that "TikTok's success hinges on its ability to addict children and teenagers to the platform" and that the company "knowingly deceives parents and allows children to be exposed to harmful and inappropriate content in direct violation of Florida law." The lawsuit alleges TikTok misrepresents the content available on its platform, downplaying the prevalence of sexual content, drug use, profanity, self-harm and eating disorders despite marketing the app as appropriate for users 13 and older. The state also contends that TikTok engages in deceptive and unfair trade practices by misleading parents about platform safety and content moderation, while being aware of the risks posed to young users.

cards.headline: Florida Medicaid enrollment dips below pre-pandemic levels as CHIP numbers drop 31%
cards.teaser: Florida's combined Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program enrollment has fallen slightly below pre-pandemic levels, with child enrollment in CHIP declining sharply.
cards.body:
Florida's combined Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program enrollment has dipped slightly below pre-pandemic levels, according to February 2026 data compiled by KFF. The state had 3.58 million Floridians enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP as of February, down from 3.60 million in February 2020, before the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted enrollment patterns nationwide. Florida is among a minority of states where combined enrollment has fallen below the February 2020 baseline. Nationally, Medicaid and CHIP enrollment remains 5% above pre-pandemic levels.

Child enrollment in Medicaid and CHIP fell from 2.41 million in February 2020 to 2.30 million in February 2026, a decline of roughly 107,000 children or 4%. Adult enrollment increased to 1.28 million from 1.19 million before the pandemic, an increase of about 87,000 adults or 7%. The most significant decline occurred within CHIP, where enrollment dropped from 240,730 children to 165,278 in February, a 31% decrease. Medicaid enrollment alone remains slightly above pre-pandemic levels at 3.41 million in February 2026, up from 3.36 million. The CHIP decline comes amid Florida's ongoing dispute over a federal rule requiring 12 months of continuous eligibility for children enrolled in the program, even if their parents miss a premium payment. This dispute has delayed implementation of a 2023 law expected to expand eligibility to about 40,000 children.

cards.headline: Johnson & Johnson investing $1 billion in Jacksonville manufacturing facility
cards.teaser: The healthcare giant will expand its Vision Manufacturing facility on Jacksonville's Southside, part of a larger $55 billion U.S. investment plan.
cards.body:
Johnson & Johnson officials announced a $1 billion investment to expand the company's Vision Manufacturing facility in Jacksonville. The funding will support construction of an upgraded distribution facility and expansion of manufacturing and packaging technologies to meet growing demand for eye healthcare products. The Jacksonville factory, which has operated on the Southside for years, primarily produces contact lens technology and serves an estimated 40 million patients in the U.S. and worldwide. Company officials expect the new distribution facility to be fully operational in 2028.

Chair and CEO Joaquin Duato said the investment reinforces the company's conviction that advanced manufacturing in the United States is essential to delivering innovative, high quality healthcare solutions to patients. The Jacksonville project is part of a larger company commitment of $55 billion into U.S. operations to improve manufacturing, research and technology through 2029. Johnson & Johnson estimates it has a $6 billion annual economic impact in Florida with about 3,500 employees in the Jacksonville area. Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan called the investment "a strong vote of confidence in Jacksonville, our workforce, and our future."

cards.headline: State Rep. Paula Stark exploring legal challenge after disqualification from HD 47 ballot
cards.teaser: The St. Cloud Republican says she was disqualified over financial disclosure paperwork that had already been filed electronically the day before the deadline.
cards.body:
State Rep. Paula Stark says she is working on a legal challenge after being disqualified as a candidate for re-election in House District 47. The St. Cloud Republican said election officials knocked her off the ballot over a failure to file financial disclosures that had already been accepted electronically a day beforehand through the Commission of Ethics portal. Stark said she has a digitally accepted receipt from the COE available online. She alleged that a disruption at the Division of Elections office on Friday, the qualifying deadline, may have impacted the process when security was removing an individual causing a disturbance, creating a backlog of close to a dozen candidates waiting to submit paperwork. The Division of Elections shifted her status to "did not qualify" shortly after the Friday noon deadline, though Stark submitted her partisan candidate oath at 11:35 a.m. and a check for her qualifying fee at 11:37 a.m.

The only candidates to qualify for House District 47 were Jorge Figueroa, president of the Puerto Rican Chamber of Commerce of Central Florida, and Anthony Nieves, a former state investigator. If they remain the only two qualified candidates, a Primary on Aug. 18 will be open to all voters and decide the Representative for the next two years, resulting in a pickup for Democrats in the House. Stark defeated Nieves by 878 votes in 2022 during a red wave year and retained the seat in 2024. The Division of Elections has no appeals process for disqualifications, leaving the courts as the only recourse.

cards.headline: Study finds Florida pharmacies expanded adult vaccine access but gaps remain
cards.teaser: A new national report examining vaccine access laws finds Florida has expanded the role pharmacies play in administering adult vaccines but still falls short of some advocate recommendations.
cards.body:
A new report examining vaccine access laws nationwide finds Florida has expanded the role pharmacies play in administering adult vaccines, but still falls short of policies advocates say would further improve access. The study, produced by Manatt Health for the American Disease Prevention Coalition, reviews pharmacy vaccination authority across all 50 states and concludes that significant differences remain in how states authorize pharmacists, pharmacy interns and pharmacy technicians to administer vaccines. In Florida, pharmacy interns are permitted to administer adult vaccines under the supervision of a pharmacist, while pharmacy technicians may also administer vaccines with authority limited to adult immunizations. The study notes nearly 90% of states now allow pharmacy technicians to administer vaccines, up from fewer than 30% in 2021, with the number of states authorizing pharmacy technicians to vaccinate growing from 14 in 2021 to 46 in 2024.

Researchers found that community pharmacies have become an increasingly important point of access for vaccinations, noting that 93% of Americans live within five miles of a pharmacy. The report identifies three policy approaches it says would improve adult vaccine access: broadly authorizing FDA-approved or CDC-recommended adult vaccines, reducing prescription and physician protocol requirements, and allowing trained pharmacy interns and technicians to administer the same adult vaccines as pharmacists under appropriate supervision. Kayla McFeely, vice president of Health and Wellness Strategy and Policy for the National Association of Chain Drug Stores, noted that pharmacies help address access barriers by offering walk-in appointments, extended hours and convenient locations.

cards.headline: Florida university faculty political donations skew heavily Democratic, study finds
cards.teaser: An analysis of political contributions by faculty and staff at Florida's five largest public universities shows nearly nine of every 10 dollars donated went to Democratic candidates and committees during the 2024 federal election cycle.
cards.body:
An analysis of political contributions by faculty and staff at Florida's five largest public universities found that nearly nine of every 10 dollars donated went to Democratic candidates and committees during the 2024 federal cycle. The study examined donations at Florida International University, Florida State University, the University of Central Florida, the University of Florida and the University of South Florida using the Federal Election Commission's public database, which requires disclosure of employer for donations exceeding $200.

Counting individual donations rather than dollars, the Democratic share ranged from 71% at FIU to 89% at UCF. The analysis also examined donors who clearly favored one party, directing at least 65% of their contributions to that party. At every school, more than 80% of those donors favored Democrats. Faculty and staff donated to Democratic committees at more than twice the rate of Florida donors generally, and by dollars, they directed money to Democrats at roughly four-and-a-half times the rate of their fellow Floridians. Ryan Owens, director of the Institute for Governance and Civics at FSU, noted that the analysis has limits, examining only the 2024 election cycle and only donations exceeding $200. The findings align with research by professors Jon Shields and Joshua Dunn, who found that only 5% to 17% of social science faculty and 4% to 8% of humanities faculty identify as conservative.

hero.headline: Driver dies in burning vehicle near Citrus Boulevard in Martin County
hero.teaser: A driver was found dead in a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court on Saturday night.
hero.body:
A fatal vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court in Martin County is being investigated as a possible accidental ignition, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded just after 9 p.m. Saturday to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road. When first responders arrived, they found the driver deceased inside the vehicle, burned beyond recognition.

The incident was initially treated as a traffic crash-related fire. However, after further investigation at the scene, detectives ruled out a collision as the cause, prompting the involvement of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives tentatively identified the victim and have been in contact with family members. However, due to the condition of the remains, positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed. Those results are expected to take several weeks.

cards.headline: Brush fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County extinguished
cards.teaser: A fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County was extinguished with help from multiple agencies.
cards.body:
Multiple agencies responded to a fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County. The fire was extinguished with assistance from several responding units.

The Florida Forest Service reported that a wildlife fire in Martin County covering over 100 acres was contained. Additional reports indicated a brush fire briefly slowed traffic on I-95 northbound in Palm City before it was brought under control.

cards.headline: Palm City brush fire on I-95 northbound fully contained
cards.teaser: A brush fire that briefly slowed traffic on I-95 northbound in Palm City is now 100% contained.
cards.body:
A brush fire near I-95 northbound in Palm City caused brief traffic delays before being brought under control. The fire is now 100% contained, according to reports.

The Florida Forest Service confirmed that the over 100-acre fire in Martin County was fully contained. Multiple agencies assisted in extinguishing the blaze.

cards.headline: Florida Forest Service reports over 100-acre fire in Martin County contained
cards.teaser: The Florida Forest Service confirmed that an over 100-acre wildlife fire in Martin County has been contained.
cards.body:
The Florida Forest Service reported that a wildlife fire covering more than 100 acres in Martin County was contained. Multiple agencies responded to the fire, which affected the area near Newfield Parkway.

The containment effort came as a brush fire near Palm City also briefly slowed northbound traffic on I-95 before being fully extinguished.

cards.headline: 2026 election candidates filing in Martin County
cards.teaser: Candidates are filing to run in the 2026 elections in Martin County, Florida.
cards.body:
The 2026 election cycle is underway in Martin County as candidates file to run for various positions. Information on who is running in Martin County is being compiled as the filing period continues.

Voters in Martin County will have the opportunity to review candidate information as the election approaches in November 2026.

cards.headline: Investigation continues into Martin County vehicle fire death
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office continues to investigate the death of a driver found in a burning vehicle.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is continuing its investigation into a fatal vehicle fire that occurred Saturday night. A driver was found dead inside a burning vehicle off the side of the road near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court.

Investigators believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. The investigation remains ongoing as detectives work to determine the full circumstances of the incident.

hero.headline: Film production scheduled to begin in Fort Pierce on June 26
hero.teaser: A film titled 'As For Me & My House, Sundays Is For Church' is scheduled to begin filming in Fort Pierce and Rockledge.
hero.body:
The film 'As For Me & My House, Sundays Is For Church' is scheduled to begin filming on June 26, 2026, in Fort Pierce. The production will continue on June 27, 2026, in Rockledge.

The filming schedule indicates Fort Pierce will host the first day of production for the project. No additional details about the film's content or production crew were provided in the announcement.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie council votes to distribute $24 million Waste Pro settlement via tax roll
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city leaders voted 4-1 Monday to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the tax roll rather than sending checks to residents. The tax roll option allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties using an established system. Council members also voted against reimbursing the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund. The settlement resolved lawsuits filed by both the city and Waste Pro in 2021, with Waste Pro blaming labor shortages and the city arguing the company breached its contract for standard of service.

Resident Kelly Lee, who attended Monday's meeting, recalled trash troubles during the pandemic when Waste Pro failed to pick up overflowing garbage. She raised concerns about fair distribution, noting that some residents who dealt with the trash problems have since moved while new residents now live in their homes. Lee questioned where the fair share goes for people who were present during the issues but have since relocated. Scott Samples with the city said staff have been working to collect data and create scenarios to give recommendations to city council. Mayor Shannon Martin stated in April after the settlement announcement that she was committed to making sure residents get paid back for what they endured during that time.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie city council votes to distribute $24 million Waste Pro settlement via tax roll
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie city leaders voted 4-1 to distribute funds via the tax roll from the $24 million settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro, choosing that option over sending checks to residents.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie city council voted 4-1 to distribute the $24 million settlement from former trash hauler Waste Pro by crediting the funds directly to properties via the tax roll. This method uses an established system to channel the money to residents rather than issuing individual checks. Council members also decided against reimbursing the city for emergency solid waste expenses that had been covered by the general fund during the service failures.

The settlement stems from years of trash collection problems that plagued the city during the pandemic. Waste Pro failed to pick up overflowing bins regularly, leaving trash piled up on residents' yards. Both the city and Waste Pro filed lawsuits against each other in 2021. Waste Pro blamed labor shortages for the service failures, while the city argued the company breached its contract by failing to maintain adequate service standards. The dispute ultimately resulted in the $24 million settlement agreement.

Kelly Lee, a Port St. Lucie resident, attended Monday's council meeting to weigh in on how the money should be distributed. She recalled the frustration neighbors experienced when their trash accumulated as "a stinky mess" on their yards due to missed pickups. However, Lee raised concerns about fairness in the distribution process. She questioned how the city would handle compensation for people who experienced the problems but have since moved away, as well as for newer residents who were not impacted by Waste Pro's failures. "People have moved, the residents are no longer here, some of them are brand new residents that didn't pay into waste pro," Lee said, asking where those who left would receive their fair share.

Scott Samples with the city acknowledged the complexity of the situation, noting that staff have been working to collect data and develop different distribution scenarios for council recommendations. He emphasized that the city's goal is to make the best possible decision that helps address the hardship residents endured during that period. Mayor Shannon Martin previously stated her commitment to ensuring residents receive compensation for their troubles. Lee urged city leaders to involve residents in the decision-making process. "Have us weigh in on something to at least feel part of the process. One size can't fit all," she said.

cards.headline: Proposed homestead exemption expansion could shift property tax burden to renters, critics warn
cards.teaser: A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could lower tax bills for homeowners, but an analysis estimates Martin County could lose more than $67 million in revenue.
cards.body:
A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could lower tax bills for homeowners, but critics worry renters may face higher costs if local governments raise rates to offset lost revenue. A Florida Policy Institute analysis estimates Martin County could lose more than $67 million if the amendment passes in November, with statewide losses reaching nearly $4.8 billion. Mike Readling, executive director of Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, says 95% of people seeking his organization's help with rent and bills are renters who would not benefit from the tax cut. "The housing situation is so dire. It's gotten progressively worse. We have families coming in everyday," Readling said.

If local governments face revenue shortfalls, attorney John Tolley says they could cut services, dip into reserves, or raise millage rates. Realtor Michael Caputo noted that homesteaded homeowners would still benefit from the tax break even if rates rise, but landlords without the exemption could face higher bills and potentially increase rents. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis found only 24 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income renters. The amendment would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10% to 5%. Tolley suggested lower taxes on rentals could actually reduce rents, while Caputo said landlords would adjust pricing based on market demand.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens woman receives toll bills after husband's temporary tag stolen
cards.teaser: Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens has received multiple toll bills from Florida's Gulf Coast after someone used a temporary tag registered to her husband on a black Mercedes.
cards.body:
Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens received a toll bill in March for multiple tolls along Florida's Gulf Coast with a license plate number matching a temporary tag registered to her husband. The bill referenced a black Mercedes with a photograph, but the Keswicks drive a white Nissan that has had a permanent tag for months. Keswick-Paine filed a report with Palm Beach Gardens Police and expressed concern about potential criminal liability. "The guy runs a red light, the tag is in my husband's name. The guy hits and runs, tag is under my husband's name," she said. Palm Beach Gardens Police said in an email they consider the case isolated, but personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti said the problem is far more common. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement does not have statewide data on stolen temp tags immediately available.

Following police advice, Keswick-Paine did not pay the bill and filed a dispute with SunPass instead. A second invoice arrived anyway, and SunPass eventually closed the dispute, but Keswick-Paine said she could not get confirmation the matter was resolved. She received a third toll bill after reaching out to the Florida Department of Transportation in April. Security consultant and retired police officer Gene Petrino said the nature of temp tag fraud makes it difficult to investigate. He advised keeping thorough records of police reports and toll disputes, and destroying temp tags by cutting them into pieces when transitioning to permanent license plates. A new Florida law that kicked in last year increased penalties for fraudulent use of temp tags and made them easier for the state to track.

cards.headline: Belle Glade residents voice housing concerns, share community stories at library meetup
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library for a Let's Hear It community meetup, sharing stories about housing affordability, l.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library during a Let's Hear It community meetup to share stories about housing affordability, local resources, and upcoming events. Much of the conversation centered on affordability and housing challenges facing the community. Local activist Delories Butts raised concerns about homelessness, asking why the community cannot help homeless people. Other residents expressed positive feelings about living in Belle Glade, with resident Veronica Bain saying, "I love it. I love it."

Residents also learned about available community resources and upcoming celebrations. Lavita Holmes, executive director of Glades Lives Matter, described the organization's ambassadorship program, which selects three students from every school to mentor throughout the year. The program holds students civically responsible for attending school board meetings and commission meetings to stay informed about their communities. Holmes explained that the organization serves as "a voice for the people that reside in the Glades community." Codi Snead announced the first Juneteenth pageant in the county's history, currently featuring eight contestants in grades kindergarten through fifth. Residents interested in sharing their concerns can email LetsHearIt@wptv.com.
